utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You may recall yesterday we closed by discussing the Markale incident and we had just discussed the direction of fire and the angle of descent and were just about to move on to the possible positions -- the possible firing positions. If you could -- you still have your reports, I see.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you could move to pages -- well, firstly page 13 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In which report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This is the Markale report. That's 65 ter 03119. I believe that's Exhibit P588.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Higgs, in your report you have indicated that there were four possibilities the mortar could have been fired from. If you see charge one, 900 metres; charge 2, 1600 metres; charge 3, 2.400 metres; and charge 4, 3.000 metres. Out of those four ranges, which, in your opinion, was the distance from where the mortar was fired?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From looking at the case, the most likely charge would have been charge 3, in a range of approximately 2400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you to just mark on the map that is on the next page the rough locations at these distances, would you be able to do that, at least for charge 1, charge 2, and charge 3? And I'm going to ask you some further questions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page, please, page 13 and there's a map. And if that map could be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You have the map there on the screen, Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that line -- well, is that the direction from which the shell came from, the 170 degrees that you concluded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the approximate direction that the round came in from, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Firstly, and if you require a ruler, I think there is one in the court. Could you mark where 2400 metres would be from the incident location that is the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2400 metres would be somewhere in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 1600 metres, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would be in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The red line, you see the red dotted line, to your knowledge what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red dotted line and the blue dotted line that run parallel to each are is the position of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the territory that is below the red dotted line therefore to the bottom of the picture, which party to the conflict controlled that territory ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would be the Serb forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And above the blue line, would that be the ABiH forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, do you also -- from your review of the material, are you able to roughly locate the position of the UN observer at that time? And if you can, just please put a cross.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN observer was on the high ground in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said your conclusion was that it came from 2,400 metres away. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having ascertained the direction, then by looking at the map, if the round had been fired from 900 metres, this puts that location very close to an urban area where there would be lots of people who could have heard the firing, and there was no report that anyone heard that firing. Then when you come back to 600 metres it places it right between the confrontation lines, which would be totally tactically sound for the position of a mortar and again very close in direct line of hearing from the UN observer, so you should have heard it. And then when you back to the area of 2400, you are now coming back to the more ideal position where a mortar would want to be, on the higher ground. It is far enough away from the confrontation line for tactical reasons for survivability. Plus, because it is up there in the hills, steep hills, it is shrouded from the UN observer by these hills, and so therefore, of course, that would reduce the chance of any sound being heard when fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to just concentrate on a few factors that you mentioned in your answer. Firstly let's talk about the sound. In your experience, how far can one be from a 120-millimetre mortar, given that the conditions are fair, to hear it being fired?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fair conditions you could hear the sound probably up to three to even four kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And again, the UN observer, roughly on this map, how far was the observer from -- let's say if it was fired from 1600 metres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only about one kilometre away from that line of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would intervening landscapes such as hills make a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Obviously hills between the firing and the person hearing would make a big difference. But on looking at the map here, between the hill that the UN observer was on, the range is of 900 and 1600. There is not a hill higher in between that particular line of fire. Only when you go beyond 1600 do you come into the taller hills and the mountain ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you said that if it was at 1600 metres it would be tactically unsound. Just explain why you think it would be tactically unsound to place mortars in that position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That position there would put this particular mortar either right on the front line or even in between the two front lines. For such a valuable asset, to place it in such a vulnerable position would not make tactical sense. The 120-millimetre mortar is a large piece of ordnance. Its ammunition is heavy. Ideally it is resupplied by a vehicle or many, many people; and to place it in that location just would not be sensical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So given these factors that you have testified about today and also in your report, is it your firm conclusion that it was -- the most likely firing position would have been at 2.400 metres away?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who controlled the area, that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area is to the -- from this picture to the south of the red line so that would be in the Serb-held territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you this first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we move on to that next incident that you wish to mention, maybe we should ask the witness whether the Markale market is actually visible from that point of fire, because as the witness explained to us yesterday, it would be difficult to hit a particular place if you had not any observers downtown and if you cannot see the marketplace from the hills. So it is of importance to ascertain whether the market could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, well, firstly just answer that question: In your view is it possible to -- for the mortar battery operator to see the marketplace in that location of 2.400 metres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that area, you cannot see the market itself because it is hidden by the taller buildings all around it. But you can identify the taller buildings very easily. For instance the cathedral is not far from that location and the other taller buildings. So you could use those as reference points to assist you, but you cannot see the marketplace itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that. But could you see the downtown area from there or would it be hidden by hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You can see the buildings, you can see the downtown area. The area of 2400, that is the tallest hill in that area. So you're looking down on to the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Higgs, from your evidence yesterday, leaving aside whether a target can be seen, is it your opinion - well, you've actually stated your opinion, but would there have been targets that would have been pre-recorded at this time of the conflict, that is August, 1995 in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my opinion, by this stage they would have had many reference points pre-recorded to make the fire more accurate and to save wasting ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And therefore, hypothetically would it still have been possible to hit the market place in a single round, given the factor of pre-recorded targets, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is going to make the chance of doing that a lot greater. If not a direct hit, then one very close could definitely be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, given the fact that this was a single round at the marketplace, do you have an opinion as to whether there was a military objective to this -- to this course of action?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot gain any definite military action from firing just a single round. The military have what is known as harassing fire, which is designed to prevent an enemy from basically moving in an area, which is normally a combination of rounds fired over a longer period of time, so that people don't like moving around in that particular area, because they don't know when the next one's going to arrive. A single round would not really make that happen, so there's not a lot of military objective to be gained from firing a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, thus, with this round that was fired, what is your opinion as to the -- the purpose of firing this round? What would be the, let's say the intention of the person who fired the round, or the army that fired the round?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firing a single round into a, as in this case, centre of a built-up area at or close to an area where civilians are known to be present would probably be more on the lines of to terrorise the population and to actually kill civilian casualties rather than any military objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I just want to take you back very briefly to follow up on one more point that His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you. With respect to observers, and again generally this doesn't, as you have stated, does not apply to this incident, but would an observer have to be at the target or would -- or would the target have to be in the line of sight of an observer, irrespective of where the observer is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we spoke about yesterday, if the mortar could have direct line of sight itself, it could do direct fire. However, if it using indirect fire, the observer could have been anywhere around the town of Sarajevo, not necessarily on this line of sight at all. They could have been anywhere to the north, south, east or west, because it's possible then for the observer to bring fire in no matter where they are located.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question on this incident: In your opinion, was this incident the result of a static explosion at the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From looking at the patterns generated on the road, identified it as a mortar round, there was no secondary marks, any secondary explosion, or secondary means of ignition, which there would have been if you had placed some form of explosive on a round and then placed it in that position. Also, if this round was put there statically, it would have to have been held in some sort of frame to hold it at approximately 70 degrees, and there was no evidence of any secondary debris reported on the site of whatever that would have been held in, and also there's been no reports of somebody placing something that I have seen in the middle of this road, which would have taken some time then to set up in plain view of everybody prior to detonating. So, for all those reasons, I doubt it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say secondary marks, are you saying that there would have been an additional device to the actual mortar projectile that would have caused marks on the -- on the crater on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they had used a 120-millimetre bomb statically, then it needed to be detonated in some way, either by placing a secondary charge on the side, which would have affected the pattern tremendously, or by possibly removing the fuse and placing some charge where the fuse normally would have been, again wasn't the case, because the Bosnian authorities found fuse fragments at the site, so the fuse was there. So for those reasons, it's unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that it would have taken some time to set up in plain view of everyone. How much time are we speaking about here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's difficult to estimate. Because, again it would have had to have some sort of frame to hold the round at the particular angle, pointing then the -- that particular frame into the direction that you wanted the round to have come from, at the angle that you wanted to represent, and then have some form of frame that holds the round that isn't going to give any signs that it was even there after the round exploded is not something probably you're going to set up in a couple of minutes. It probably is going to take a longer period of time than that so set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry I keep saying that I'm going leave this incident, but I do have one more question. You said that, in your view, the location of 2.400 metres would have been at a high point where the town, let's say, the centre of town would have been visible. When you say "high point," does that elevation - I know you've answered this before yesterday, but would that elevation affect the range at which the mortar could be -- that the mortar could be fired? Would it increase or decrease the range ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have increased the possible range of the mortar because an increasing elevation above point of impact would give the mortar a slightly longer range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as I did yesterday with the photograph, I would just like you with your pen to -- you see the arrow of 170 degrees. You have the arrow pointing towards the bottom of the picture. I just would like to you mark on that line the arrow from -- in the direction from which the projectile came into the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this still into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Higgs, if we can swiftly move on to the second incident, and that is the one at Livanjska Street and the shelling at 1525 hours. And that's contained in your second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that would be 65 ter 013120. And if we could move to page 8 of the English and also page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, in this incident, this is the earlier incident at Livanjska Street, do you recall whether the crater was on the pavement or on the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this instance, the round had landed on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from the review of the photographs, were you able to come to an understanding as to whether the tail-fin was lodged in the crater or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case the tail-fin was still in the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And would the pavement have been softer or harder ground than the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally the pavements, because of their construction, are generally softer construction than a main road, which is probably why we had the tail-fin still in the crater in this case, as opposed to the later one which landed in the road when that was then not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the fact that the tail-fin was lodged in the crater in this incident, what, in your opinion, would that tend to indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conjunction with the rest of the investigation that was carried out and the tail-fins being in the crater, it tends to indicate that the mortar was probably fired on a higher charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just again explain, when you say "higher charge," how does that affect the range? Was it fired from a farther or shorter distance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The angle of descent that was calculated in the investigations, it would have meant ones fired from a longer distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your review of the materials that were provided and also the -- your own analysis of the photographs, were you satisfied as to the calculation of the direction of fire on this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at both the investigations, and both methodologies in these cases were sound and they both came up to the same conclusions as to angle of descent and the general direction. I've got no reason to disagree with those two investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you come to a conclusion as to a possible firing position for this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the most logical firing position for this one, taking into account the angle of descent, the position of the tail-fins, the mortar was probably fired on a charge put in a position just north of the confrontation line I see on the map, somewhere in that general area, probably about five or 600 metres back from the confrontation line, in that area of I think it is Poljine in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I ask you with the assistance of the usher just to mark with the red pen your opinion as to the possible location of the firing position.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably somewhere in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this still with the markings into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, with respect to this incident, what is your opinion as to the -- well, was there, in your opinion, a military objective to this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again in this particular case, it was a single round fired into the centre of a populated area, and for the same reasons as I said before on the Markale incident, very difficult to obtain any military objective for firing a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what, in your opinion, would have been the purpose to fire a round at this location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one again would have been to cause civilian casualties and to put basically terror into the minds of the people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, can I just confirm that this -- this still was tendered. Okay, thank you. Now I want to move to the next incident at this location, that is the two rounds that fell at 1725 on Livanjska Street. Do you recall that incident, Mr. Higgs, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in this same report that you have open, you made some conclusions and then you provided an additional report. Just very briefly explain why you provided an additional report with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first evidence I was given was the pictures especially were poor quality. They were photocopies of original photographs and from photocopies I could not really make any judgements at all. It wasn't good enough to come up with any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you then indeed receive a further set of photographs with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I then received the original photographs or copies from the originals and from that, was then able to do a more in-depth investigation of the site and produce the additional report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you able to come to calculations or conclusions that were to your satisfaction and were accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The better quality photographs were able to confirm certain points regarding this incident, and were able for me to confirm ballistic calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could now move to your additional report on this incident, and that would be 65 ter 03121. I understand it's a Prosecution Exhibit, 590. If that could be brought up on the screen, please. And if we could move to page -- page 3, please, the photographs on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, Mr. Higgs, the calculation as to direction of fire, what was your conclusion as to the direction of fire on this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From seeing the better photographs, as you can see, these now give a very good pattern which show the direction of fire, and from the top photograph on the page here, you can see that the direction of fire, it's facing toward the curb, so the round has come in from that direction over the curb. I then related that to the position of the road from the local maps and this street runs approximately north to south. By then relating the pattern of this in relation to the road, it was then impossible to confirm or deny that the two reports that we had, as to the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It was impossible to confirm or deny the two reports. Let me ask you, the UNPROFOR report, do you recall what they came to as a direction of fire calculation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR report came to a direction of approximately seventy degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how about the CSB or the Bosnian police report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The CSB report, their direction was stated in an unfamiliar way but it was stated as a bearing from 20 degrees from east. So because these two reports did not precisely agree, that's why I used these pictures to ascertain which was the more likely direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your -- in your experience and your knowledge and your expertise, is it your opinion that the Bosnian investigators made -- let's say a scientific error or was it a question about terminology?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it would have been a scientific error because the pattern of this crater a good one, and when seen in relation to the road, it is very obvious which direction it is facing. So I think it is probably a terminology error rather than a ballistic calculation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, how do you translate 20 degrees from east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally when you are talking about degrees, they will measure them from north. So 20 degrees from north would be the way I normally read it. Because they have used the term in this report, 20 degrees from east, which is different to any of the other Bosnian reports I have seen, and is nowhere near the direction of the crater, I think that it could be some confusion with -- could the person reporting on the day who has measured it from east for some reason or in translation or something. But that's why I wanted to confirm the actual direction, because this crater points a lot closer to 70 degrees than it does to 20 and 50 degrees error is one that I do not believe the Bosnian authority would have made. It is a very, very big error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it could not be read to mean 20 degrees from the east towards the north? That would make 70 degree would it not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it would. That could be where the confusion is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your review of the materials, do you recall -- and forgive me if this is a difficult question, but do you recall the place or the area where the Bosnian police suggested that the firing came from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their final report they suggested an area, please excuse my pronunciation, but, [indiscernible] area, which, I think, when marked on the map is approximately in the direction of 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for that question, but presumably if I said the name Hladivode Spicasta Stijena, would that be --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the general area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that general area corresponded to your calculation as to the direction of fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the angle of descent what -- what was your view as to the UNPROFOR calculations of the angle of descent in respect of this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I was a bit concerned here, because the Bosnian report put the angle of descent nearer 67 degrees and the UNPROFOR report was an estimate between 70 and 75 degrees. My first concern was when I saw the decent photographs is that this pattern on the ground doesn't resemble one of a 75 degrees angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there and I want you to explain that. And I explained yesterday. You see the two photographs on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If the angle of descent was 70 to 75, you said that they would be a different pattern. Where would one except to see marks on the crater if the angle was between 70 and 75?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from this pattern you have the initial burst crater and then above it you've got the -- like a fan shape which you call the second crown caused by the shrapnel. But there is very little damage as you are looking at these photographs to the bottom of the impact crater. If you remember from the crater from Markale market, which was approximately a 70 degrees angle, it was a more uniform pattern with shrapnel shape marks all around the impact crater which is what tends to happen the steeper the angle of descent becomes. This doesn't have it, so it suggests that the angle of descent on this one is probably less than 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that the crater pattern led you to the conclusion that the angle of descent would not have been as high as 70 to 75. Was there any other factor, and I'm speaking about the calculations that you spoke about yesterday, led to you your conclusion as to the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then looked at the pictures and took the calculations, the measurements from the reports which you see on the pictures here. The 110 centimetres is measured from the point of burst to the curb and then looking at the other measurements to see if I could confirm the ballistic calculations. When I started to lock at these pictures, the pictures did not agree again with the UNPROFOR measurements. The calculations as you can see in the bottom picture, on the UNPROFOR measurement they had a total measurement of the bust crater of 40 centimetres from front to rear. So from centre, point of impact to the front of the crater, would be approximately 20 centimetres as marked on that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. When you say the -- the measurement of the burst crater, 40 centimetres you basically mean -- do you mean the radius of the impact crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the diameter across the hole would be 40 centimetres, yeah. So, therefore I make it a radius of 20 centimetres from the point out. When I mark that and then looked at the map, they are a measurement from the centre of the crater to the centre of the second crown the distance L on that picture as 65 centimetres. I looked at this and thought, well, that is not three times the distance out from the centre when you look on that picture. It's only probably double the distance. It is definitely not three times further out. So probably nearer 40, 45 centimetres away from the strike, not 65 and that distance L is a key distance used in the count -- ballistics calculations. So you then recalculated using that nearer to 40, 45 centimetres and it brings you out with an angle of descent somewhere between 60, 65 degrees, opposed to 75 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with that calculation as to the angle of descent as 60 to 65, what does that indicate about the range at which the mortar was fired?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It now gives the mortar a lot longer range and now make it is possible for that mortar to have fired from a distance in excess of four kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you recall the angle of descent calculation the Bosnian police came? To.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian police in their report just put down a figure of 67 degrees but showed no workings of how they came to that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I take it from your answer, your previous answer, your calculations -- with your calculations, in your view, is the UNPROFOR report more accurate or the Bosnian report more accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Bosnian report is far more accurate, as far as angle of descent is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with this calculation and the direction of fire, did you come to a conclusion as to the possible firing point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I took this into account, with the direction coming from the area as previously stated, and also that again nobody had heard these rounds being fired because this was one of two rounds, if the rounds had been fired along this direction line, within the confrontation lines, it passes a lot of heavily built-up areas, residential areas and so on where somebody would have heard this mortar firing. However, when you get across the confrontation line in that part of Sarajevo, there's a steep escarpment, and once you've gotten over that escarpment, over the back of that, that would have muffled the sound of any mortar firing from there and then you would not have heard it. The other thing I had to take into account was the timing of this firing, which was approximately 1725 hours in November, so it would have been either dark or pitch black at that time in winter, and when a mortar fires it produces a tremendous muzzle flash or ball of flame comes out the end and this can be seen from miles away. So if it had been fired within the confrontation line, somebody would definitely have seen it. It would have been very obvious, and that's why I tended to believe that it must have come from beyond the escarpment in some form of hidden low-lying ground beyond the hill to prevent anyone hearing it or seeing the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Higgs, I'm -- maybe we will get back to this question at a later point, but I cannot help putting it to you at this point, and the question is: How do you compensate for the lack of knowledge of the charge used at this particular mortar, at this particular point of impact? How does one calculate the distance from where the mortar was shot when you only have the angle of descent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we only have the angle of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and of course the type of mortar used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we only have an angle of descent to the type of mortar, of course the mortar could achieve that angle of descent on all charges. So then we have to look at the lay of the land and just use experience and look at the obvious positions and when you look at all the other charges to fire, it puts the mortar, say in built-up areas very close to residential areas or on -- not until you really get to the areas to the north of Sarajevo where the hills are do you come to really what would a good mortar position. And then try and look at other evidence like has anybody heard the firing or not, and from all that, try and come up with an educated opinion of where the round would come from. But, yes you are right. The mortar can of course achieve this angle of descent on all six charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, can I just ask you: This educated opinion that you're speaking about, is this something that you have done in your career on numerous occasions when you haven't been able to identify the charge being used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I was just going to conclude this incident by asking you -- and you have probably answered this, but just to be clear, in your view, was the round fired from territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb army or territory controlled by the Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking the position which I believe the mortar was fired from, this would have been territory held by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is your opinion as to the possible purpose or the objective of firing this round and of course you recall there was a further round in the garden sometime later, a few minutes later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one -- again a single round into a residential area on to a road would achieve little as far as a military objective is concerned. What is a little bit concerning is the time delay to the second round. A mortar is capable of firing rounds very quickly. An 82-millimetre mortar like this can probably fire 20 rounds a minute on maximum rates of fire, so you can fire rounds only seconds apart. But in this case here there was several minutes passed between the first and the second explosion. One reason why sometimes this happens is that if you fire a first one into an area knowing you're going to cause a casualty, what tends to happen, of course, is the local authorities, whoever they be, will then come around the area and of course treat casualties and so. You then wait a period of time, five, ten minutes, and fire a second one in the area, knowing that you're going to then catch probably more people in the area than was there in the first place. It's a tactic that is used by terrorist organizations with bombs, for instance, by having two in the same area a few minutes apart. Obviously. I cannot prove that is the case here, but there would be no military objective by firing them let's say at about a five, ten-minute delay apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's assume that you're actually targeting a particular point so you shoot your first -- you fire your first round and you see where that land in your binoculars and then you adjust your -- the mortar -- the position, how long time does that normally take to adjust, you know, a little bit to left, a little bit to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're trying to go for a particular point, yes, we call what you mentioned there, we adjust the fire onto the target, so you would fire the first one. The observer would then see the round fall, make his corrections, send that to the mortar, and then they would fire another adjusting round onto hopefully a more accurate target. That, depending on the skill of the observer, and the detachment could take anything from between two minutes to possibly ten minutes, depending on their skill. But of course you then expect the second round to be a lot closer to the target or the point of aim. This particular second round landed in somebody's back garden not far from the first one, so it didn't appear that they were adjusting it on to any other military-type target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on page 19, line 10 you're saying that the report of the Bosnian authorities was more accurate than that of the UNPROFOR, concerning the angle of descent. And since we know that the angle of descent is important in order to calculate not only the origin, the direction of fire, but also the distance covered, would you say that the conclusion as to the distance and hence the origin of fire was the same in the two reports that is, the Bosnian report and that of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian report put the angle of descent closer to 67 degrees, but the UNPROFOR report had it as an estimate between 70 and 75 degrees, and again by looking at these pictures and some of the basic calculations that I carried out, I believe that the Bosnian report, 67 degrees is a far more accurate report as far as angle of descent is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, perhaps if I can just follow up one question from His Honour Judge Mindua and possibly to clarify. The initial -- in other words, before you received the set of photographs do you recall that the UNPROFOR report, based on their calculations as to the angle of descent, concluded -- in fact it's covered on page 10 in your second report -- concluded that the round would have come from some 3.200 -- in other words, a possible range extended to only 3.200 metres. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And does that range correspond to an angle descent of -- sorry, correspond to their calculations for the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is worked off their angle of descent of approximately 75 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And therefore just be clear, your conclusion as to the angle of descent once you reviewed the new photographs and made those calculations of 65 to 60 degrees, would that take the range beyond 3.200 metres and therefore beyond the confrontation, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would make a big difference to range and it would have made it possible for the round to come well beyond the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could now move to the last incident, and that is the incident at Dobrinja on the 18th of June. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what -- after the review -- after your review of the materials, what was your conclusion as to the possible direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, on this report here, I have got no reason to disbelieve the Bosnian report and the bearing that they came up with. Indeed, in this case because of the buildings surrounding the water point where this incident occurred, there was only one direction available where the round could have come from, and that agrees with the explanation in the Bosnian report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In other words -- well, let me ask you: What is your opinion as to the methdology employed by the Bosnians in undertaking this investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All their methodologies used for this particular case were sound, because this was a difficult case due to the fact that the round landed halfway up a wall and did not impact on the ground. So it was more of a case of eliminating what could not have happened is what they carried out and that's why they then come up with that general bearing of the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On page 19 of the report, that is the second report, 65 ter 03120, you -- you say that the Bosnian authorities came to the conclusion that the fire came from Nedzarici, the Nedzarici region. And you conclude that this is indeed the most likely firing position. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the direction from which the round came from. So direction is not really in doubt. The -- as far as the range is concerned, that particular region and its distance away would have meant that the -- the mortar could have fired on a reasonably low charge, which are the most accurate charges for any mortar to fire, to guarantee a more accurate hit on the target. If you then put the -- find a position further away, the mortar would had to have fired of course on the higher charges, and its accuracy then of course would have been degraded. So that particular region is the most likely firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And now I'm finished. I just -- and I apologise for this. I want to going back to Prosecution Exhibit 594. I seem to recall that I want you to make one more marking just so the evidence is properly recorded and then I'll be finished, Mr. President. Mr. Higgs, you recognise this still?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I would just like you, with a pen, the larger circle, I understand, is the 2.400 metres -- I would like you to write 2.400 metres next to that circle and then just put underneath that FP for "firing position," please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Higgs. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Higgs, my name is Branislav Tapuskovic. I represented Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. Following this examination-in-chief I too have questions for you myself. So that we may clarify any remaining issues in relation to your report. First of all, a brief question about P588. This is an OTP document, the report, the date is the 3rd of August, 2006. It addresses certain features of your profession and your familiarity with the subject matter. So this is the report that you provided, right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to dwell for a moment on this introduction. We were talking about Markale and I have to go back to this report. In your introduction you state all of your jobs. You were the quartermaster sergeant instructor with the Small Arms School Corps, you were with the mortar division, and you also state that you worked in civilian environments or settings, too, as far as I understand, studying the effects of mortar shells. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never provided any assessments about mortar fire as a result of a war or within a war. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only assessments in war would be the ones relating to the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, since you didn't have that sort of experience, and as far as I can tell, you never completed any schools where you would have had a chance to study mortar fire in such a way that the Trial Chamber in this trial might find useful. Would that not seem be to the case, or, rather, sir, can you explain more about your training in addition to the military training and your daily military activities, what exactly do you know about ballistics and everything else that work of this nature normally involves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have asked about four questions. You are to ask one question at a time. What is the question that you wish to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to cut this short, it's about the background and the qualifications with regard to mortar fire. That really is my only question. The background, any schools in relation to that. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just note for the record that in the Defence response to our 94 bis submission to have Mr. Higgs as an expert, the Defence did not notify the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber that they intended to cross-examine on Mr. Higgs' qualifications and expertise. I just note that for the record, as required by the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 94 bis, are you familiar with that, Mr. Tapuskovic, testimony of expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar all of the three experts that we have heard so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You see, one of the purposes of the rule is to avoid time-wasting. Why didn't you notify that you wished to cross-examine the expert in relation to his expertise? Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. President. However, the Prosecution has no problem with the witness defending his qualifications. It's just simply to notify the Trial Chamber that the procedure was not appropriately followed, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But they did notify that they wished to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the rule does specifically state that if they want to challenge the qualifications and expertise, it should be noted. However, the Prosecution reiterates that we have no problem with Mr. Higgs defending his qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in the circumstances, Mr. Higgs, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my experience in military, I -- in my position as divisional instructor I was responsible for all mortar training within the British Army. That included all live firing. I was responsible for the total safety of all mortar firing which involved all use with mortar templates, ballistic calculations. I was also responsible for carrying out all scenes of crime investigation in criminal cases involving mortars where there had been casualties or deaths caused with British service people anywhere around the world. I also conducted these investigations for other foreign armies, using my expertise, and trained some of their ballistic experts on how to carry out mortar investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's it, that's your training? That is everything you did. You trained others. What I'm asking you is your education, that sort of background. What a sort of education do you have in order to be able to train others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was in my instructor role, I was trained within the artillery, which my training lasted a couple of years initially and then worked in artillery. When I then transferred across to mortars, I had to attend four separate training courses, basic mortar courses lasting about 12 weeks and then advanced mortar courses lasting up to 20 weeks which I had to attend two. I then had to do my instructor qualification which was a year in length. I then to do mortar investigation and artillery investigation courses, many of these, most of them probably six to eight weeks in length individually. I then had to do my training as a warrant officer in the SESC, which is technical, again, training, lasting approximately nine months. I also then did lots of short courses and training with mortar and ammunition manufacturers from all over the world, and this -- then coupled with working solidly in mortars for just over 11 years and doing nothing else, gave me the experience and the knowledge then, where I was sought after to give that experience, as I said, to many foreign countries and commercial concerns and all technical matters relating to mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could please move on. I want to move on to page 6 of the B/C/S. I'm talking about the same report. I think this is page 7 in the English, where you discuss the Sarajevo area. You state here that you visited the town before, including the area in the indictment. When you say "before," can you try to be more specific, please. When exactly do you mean? Do you mean just before you produced the reports or at the time of writing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Sarajevo before the first case that I was on, so that would be in 2002 as we spoke about yesterday and visited all the local areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you served -- or you testified as an expert in the Galic trial as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You provided an expert report regarding the Markale 1 incident, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, talking about the 28th of August, 1995, your position is the same as that regarding events that occurred on the 5th of February, 1995. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Markale 1 incident, the firing came from a different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please stop. Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just would ask perhaps for more specificity when he asks is his position the same does he mean with respect to -- well, what does he mean in respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Fair enough. Be a little more specific. On the 5th of February in relation to what incident? Or in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that I will have sufficient time to deal with all of these matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is, because at the time you categorically stated that the shell had arrived from a position held by units of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the conclusion we came to on Markale 1, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at number 2, please, paragraph 2. "The city of Sarajevo is situated in a natural valley surrounded on all sides by high hills and can be overlooked with ease. These features make Sarajevo an ideal area for the use of indirect fire, as observation is easy." My question: Who does this apply to? Does this again apply to the army of Republika Srpska alone, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any of the forces who could get themselves onto the high features would have that advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who in most cases held those elevations or high points surrounding Sarajevo? Are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the maps that I have seen, the majority of the high vantage points were held by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about a particular elevation from which this specific shell came. These were the Republika Srpska army positions on Mount Trebevic. Is that what you stated, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the area -- just to clarify, is this the area from Markale 2 in the area of 2400?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is part of Trebevic, part of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with some of the named terms of the surrounding hills. But if that is the hills to the south that we identified in my report, then, yes, those high hills to the south were in Serb possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you know that one of the key hills in that area, several in fact, Colina Kapa and Debelo Brdo, and some others elevations were in fact, in the hands of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that they did hold some of the high hills, but when carrying out my investigations, I obviously look at the facts that I have got and then plotted on those lines so that in the maps that I got in this area of 170 degrees and in the range of 2400, it appears to be the Serb-held positions in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you generally about the next paragraph. You speak about positions from which it was possible to use indirect firing. There was this street which the -- had an open view of the buildings that could be used as reference points to make adjustments easier. Would this apply to any party in possession of these positions conducive to that type of firing, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let us move on. Another advantage to be considered was the fact that most of the mortars were in position for such a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose mortars?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mortars belonging to both of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "Their base plates were solid in the ground and all relevant targets were likely to be pre-recorded." Does that apply to both parties, as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally the last paragraph under 11. Therefore it would be safe to assume that if they wanted to hit a target within Sarajevo, then, they could easily do it." Does that, too, apply to both parties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to quickly move on to your last report, dated the 11th of March, 2007, which is several days ago. This is about the incident dated the 8th of November, 1994, at 1725 hours on that day. This is PP 00590, an OTP document. This contains some information, as well as the sources you used. You go on to state: I have been asked to look at my original report dated the 21st of December and re-examine the evidence relating to the incident, now that I have the pictures of the scene. With these new pictures, it is possible to confirm or deny the angle of descent or the bearing from which the rounds were fired in an attempt to resolve the discrepancy in the previous reports." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, page 2 in the English, you say: "The original pictures I had to work from were of poor quality." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we say, based on what I have seen so far from these documents, that only the UNPROFOR commission investigating the incident was in possession of these photographs, whereas the Bosnian side had no photographs available to them at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see how the witness can answer that as to what the Bosnian police had at the time. In fact, the photographs that were provided to the witness came from the Bosnian authorities, the better copy photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, are you in a position to say who was in possession of the -- the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know, Your Honour is that these photographs -- the better quality ones, have come from the Bosnian -- these are the Bosnian photographs as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, you received these photographs just before you started work on this report. Are these not the most recent photographs that were taken just before you embarked on your expert report. You only received this very recently. Is that not the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that question, in my submission allows for confusion. Is counsel asking whether he recently received the photographs or is counsel asking whether the witness knows whether these photographs were recently taken. They are two different questions, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Witness, when you answered "that's correct," what was that intended to respond to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I have recently received these quality photographs. I was not indicating that these are new pictures. As far as I'm aware these are pictures taken, of course, the day of the incident. It is just that I have only just prior to writing this report received these quality pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to cut this short. My question was quite specific and that is reflected in the latter part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, please, just confirm this for my benefit, sir. Once again, the photographs that you described as poor quality photographs are photographs that were in the possession of UNPROFOR, are they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The poor quality photographs I was originally given are the photographs that are in my original report, and I believe they are also Bosnian photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. I'm just trying to wrap this up as quickly as I can. Page 4 in the B/C/S; it's page 6 in the English report. You say here: "The difference between the bearings is great -- is a huge one in terms of crater analysis and no real investigator would be so far out in any bearing calculation. I therefore believe there has been a misunderstanding on how the bearing was written down and recorded from the CSB report." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the continuation of this? A direction 20 degrees from the east. This is a strange way of stating a bearing; is that not correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next, you go on to state just before the conclusion. This is page 6 in the English. In B/C/S this is page 5. In fact, it turns out that both the CSB and UNPROFOR arrived at the same conclusions and neither of the sides were wrong. "All this discrepancy in bearings can be put down to a simple misunderstanding of recorded information." Does that not mean that now all of a sudden you arrived at the conclusion that both reports were in fact accurate and identical?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of bearing, if it is just a mistranslation or a misunderstanding on this term 20 degrees, then, yes, the Bosnian report and the UNPROFOR report would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yet, despite this being your conclusion, you neglect the position of UNPROFOR. They were there at the time. They were familiar with the situation and they assessed at the time that the mortar had come in from positions held at the time by the BH army. Did they not conclude that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came to that conclusion from the very steep angle of descent they got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You find them to be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at the photographs, which is the evidence that I have reviewed and the pictures do not tend to agree with the UNPROFOR conclusions. That is why I have produced this report, because I believe that the angle of descent that the Bosnian authorities have come to seems to be far closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Despite all the errors that you have just confirmed them having made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, we discussed this angle of 20 degrees which was described as a strange way of calculating a bearing and it is contained in the CSB report and the Bosnian police report. You said yourself that that was impossible. However, you are saying now that their report actually showed exactly what you have concluded?.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Bosnian reports, as I mentioned earlier, they also give this area where they suspected the fire came from, and this area is nearer 70 degrees than the 20 in their report, which is why I believe this is some form of misrecording or translation on this 20 degrees issue, because the area on the ground they report is in line with 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break; in fact, we are past the time. So we have to adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, let us now move on to some very specific questions, which, in my view, are crucially important with regard to some of your attitudes on these incidents. Let us look at page 16 in the B/C/S version, which is page 15 in the English version. It's document P589. Page 15 in English, and I'm talking about your information report dated the 21st of December, 2006. It refers to the incident of the 18th of June, 1995, the Simon Bolivar School. I would like to direct your attention to page 15 in the English version and page 16 in the B/C/S version, where, if you can see, this paragraph which begins with: "The buildings." Can you see that, Mr. Higgs? "The buildings around the incident location." It's close to the bottom of the page in the English report. Page 15, the penultimate paragraph. "The buildings around the incident location ..."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So: "The buildings around the incident location also go to eliminate certain options when it comes to calculating the direction of fire. The buildings prevent the bomb from coming from many directions. This is explained in the drawings completed by," and now you give the name of a witness. Is this your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from -- the buildings prevent the round coming from all but one direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just recall that the witness was a protected witness, and therefore this page probably should not be broadcast that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely why I didn't mention the name and I don't think it's relevant, anyway. Now, let us look at the next page, page 16 in the English version and page 17 in the B/C/S version. It's entitled the paragraph entitled "The Correctness and Methodology of the Investigations." It reads: "In this case there was not the normal bomb crater to be able to analyse and determine direction and angle of descent. However, the buildings around the incident scene in themselves help to eliminate certain options, as the bomb could not have come from the directions where these structures were." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it fair to say that the direction from which the shells had come, if there's a building in their path, it makes it impossible to fire from that direction? Is that what stems from what you've written here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the round struck the wall, the surrounding buildings would not have allowed the bomb to have come in from any other direction than the one found in the investigation, because the buildings overhang that position and so therefore there's only one clear route in that the round had in its path.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at page 18 in the English version and page 19 in the B/C/S version. Once again, you repeat that the establishing of the bearing is facilitated by the fact that the surrounding buildings eliminate many other options. It is reasonably easy to confirm that the round came in from a westerly direction but to accurately determine the angle and bearing of descent is another matter. Again, we have difficulties presented by a building in the path of a projectile. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no building in the path of the projectile, but because it struck the wall, as it says in the report, we had no normal crater pattern and could not determine the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we must go back to page 4 of this same report, and it's page 4 in both versions, paragraph 7, which speaks about direct fire. These are your findings: "In a sense, this is a misnomer. The projectile is still fired on a high trajectory, but the target is directly visible to the mortar detachment if the sight of the mortar is used like a rifle sight, pointed straight at the target. "Direct fire from a bedded mortar is very accurate after the first round." Is this also true, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then we have again to go back to page 18 in the B/C/S version, which is page 18 in the English version. It's the chapter speaking about the reasons for the attack, deliberate or otherwise. And towards the end of this paragraph you say as follows: "In some cases a mortar can be used in the direct fire mode and in this case the person controlling the mortar aims the mortar at the target himself. To do direct fire, the operator needs to see the targets." Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will just for a moment go back to one question and we'll go back to it again later on. With regard to what you said about Markale 2 incident, which happened on the 28th of August, 1995, can you explain what can an operator see from a position where there is something between two four-story or five-story buildings, if you can't see what there is, doesn't the same apply to the incident of the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you cannot see the target or the area of the target, then the mortar will then probably be directed on to the target using an observer or firing on to a previously recorded point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come later to all the pre-recorded data. I'm asking you: How is it possible to see anything over all these buildings into the city itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are using a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Judges are conferring at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you explain how the firing takes place using an observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As mentioned earlier on, if you are using an observer, the observer by using a radio will be able to speak to the mortar, so the observer could be anywhere. He doesn't have to be anywhere near the mortar. He could be in the town, on top of a tall building, or he could be on one of the hillsides, he could very close in one of the confrontation lines, he could be anywhere where he could get a reasonable view of the target area. So he is not restricted at all where the observer can go. Then from his position he can then direct the fire anywhere he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in this particular instance this observer should have been at the place where the shell landed, given the position of those buildings. He should have been precisely at the place and the spot where the shell landed; otherwise, he couldn't explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just so the witness can answer effectively, which incident is counsel speaking about? Is it the Dobrinja incident or the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about both incidents. I haven't explained that for the benefit of the Chamber. Speaking about Dobrinja, we saw that experts adamantly stated that the buildings were blocking the view of the target. However, talking about Markale, the witness never mentioned these buildings. So I'm asking how it was possible across the whole town and the built-up area and the people who were hit there to see anything in order to engage the target as described here. So this has relevance for both incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Both incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't, in my submission, believe that the witness was saying that the buildings with respect to the Dobrinja incident were blocking the view of the target. The witness is saying that the buildings eliminate other alternatives as to direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see whether the witness can answer the question. Can you answer the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as if an observer could have seen the incident at Dobrinja, you would have to go and visit all the likely positions in all the surrounding buildings held by both forces to either confirm or deny that. I have not obviously done that, so I couldn't confirm if an observer could see that position directly or not. But on saying that, you still would need to see it directly anyway to still put accurate fire down on that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I pointed out to you page 18 in this context, and before I ask you a question about the Markale incident, in order to use a mortar, it is necessary for the target to be in sight. So what could have been seen from the position that, according to you, were at 2.400 metres, what could one have seen across the whole town and behind the buildings in terms of the person operating the sight? Can you answer me that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you cannot directly see, which was the case here, the area you wish to engage, then there are two options you have. You can use a nearby physical reference point, such as a church spire, a prominent building or something; aim your sight at that but then put a adjustment onto your sight to aim off onto the area you wish to engage, or you could use a close by pre-recorded target, if you have one, and then do a small correction from that to put the round in the area where you want it. Both of these methods are very accurate indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if we take the first one, we're working on the hypothesis that you can't see the sight, so if you use the spire of a church and then you say you make an adjustment to the target but-- but you can't see the target. I mean that's the hypothesis. So how do you make the adjustment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you would do if you cannot see it, if you were using a direct fire, the person on the site is firing the mortar himself, he will use the nearest reference point he can find. Then by using maps that he's got he'll work out the distance on the ground between his nearest reference to what he is shooting at, 100 metres or so, whatever it may be.
