Then he -- by using again the range tables, he will know what correction at that range on his sight will give that distance, and he will add it on to his sight, so that will then move the round from his reference point into the area where he wants it. That is if he is doing it by himself, i.e., by direct fire. If he's doing it by indirect fire, this a drill that the observer would do that on his behalf. His observer, using the nearest reference point, would do the calculations and send those to the mortar. So by using one or the other, you don't have to physically be able to see it to put a round very close to it. It's of course more accurate if you can see it directly. It takes away all the guesswork. But by using these calculations it is still a very accurate way of directing a round into an area that you can't directly see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Higgs, you hit a target of that nature with a single round; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good mortar detachment, if they have pre-recorded targets, should be able to put their first round either on or very, very close to the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the target is visible perhaps although I wouldn't put forward my own opinion. But in this case the target was not visible. However, according to you, it was possible to hit this invisible target with a single round.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is far easier to do this in a built up area because of all of reference points have you, especially if you have got a pre-recorded target in that area, because that target has been recorded accurately from previous fire. If you have no reference points and no pre-recorded targets, then of course it will become far more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. We shall later address the issue of pre-recorded target and corrections. Let us now focus on something that you mention regarding the purpose of the fire. Now, let us look at page 12 of the same report. That's in the B/C/S version, which is page also 12 in the English report. Here you talk about the potential intentions of the attackers and you provided an analysis saying that: "With only two rounds fired is no real military value other than harassment of the people in the area. There no are reports of any military activity in that residential area at that time. These rounds were probably aimed and fired at this location with the purpose of killing civilians. Another possible intention could be the idea of killing the authorities investigating the previous incident that day, which occurred nearby only two hours before in the same general area. And you provided a whole series of psychological analysis. Please, sir, are you qualified at all to make this kind of psychological psychiatric analysis or should it rather be within the remit of some different kind of expert? You have provided here a whole host of psychiatric and psychological analysis? Are you qualified to do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis that I have given is from my experience on operational use of mortars and teaching that to many, many different counties over the years and the correct ways of using mortars in the military environment. I have not tried to get inside the head of these people but purely relate it to military methodologies used with mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But when you speak about the psychology, sir, you are talking about fire and attackers. Who in your mind is the attacker here, or is that something that you decided in advance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I look at the evidence that I have been presented with and then try and determine from that, the type of round, direction and then from that using my experience where the round has come from. Without any prior knowledge of the sights, and I do not pre-guess what I'm going to discover. As I say, we only get certain information from the scene. I then have to use my experience and military and mortar knowledge to come to as opinion as to where the fire originated and an opinion as to its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I will be going any further into that. It's all in the report anyway. But there is one thing I would like to ask you, and I'm moving on to that. I'm going to back to what you stated, on what you wrote on page 17. This is the Simon Bolivar school building, that incident, where quite a number of people were hurt. This is 17 in the English report. And you say this: A single round was fired in this incident which leaves only one option open." And then you go on to state: "It was fired upon a group of civilians collecting water in a -- along the confrontation line in this part of the city." And then again you go on to make an assessment. This incident occurred in an area that was under the control of the BH army. Is this something that you established at the time, sir, where these civilians were injured?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by using the maps that I had, yes, it's in the BiH area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, you take the whole of page 18 to provide us with a psychological background or analysis and I'm asking you, can you provide one last like to us here? What would the case if it were proven that this particular round had come from an area under the control of the BiH army? What sort of psychological background or profile of the situation could you provide in that eventuality, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, I have got no evidence or opinion that supports that first of all. But if the evidence put the round to come from such an area, then again it would really have the same conclusion. Firing a single round on to a known position where civilians are present is obviously being down to kill civilians, to either form terror in the minds of those people, or to achieve some other wish of a commander, which I really could only guess at what that could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke similarly about the 28th of August incident, the Markale 2 incident. What I'm asking you now is to please explain to the chamber the following: Are you at all authorised to deal with these issues and to make this kind of assessment? Do you believe that this was part of your remitt when you were given this job and asked to do this job independently in order to reach an accurate and useful assessment, to do it on your own an independently, in other words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was tasked to, with the evidence presented in front of me to find or to confirm the reports I was given, their correctness and then to confirm the bearings of fire, angles of descent and then from that to find likely firing positions. I was also then asked from the type of rounds fired and their numbers what would be the probable likely intentions, i.e., military likely intentions and that is what I have done in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your assignment was the same when you appeared in the Galic trial as an expert?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The psychological profiles that you provided in that trial were identical to these, were they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't provide psychological profiles. I just gave, in my opinion, the possible military intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you for that correction. The witness did not provide psychological profiles. I think that is an improper characterisation of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant the assessments that I read. It wasn't my intention to tire the Chamber with these lengthy pages containing all these lengthy explanations. We shall, if time enough for that during our Defence case. But what I meant to ask this witness was whether, he, in fact carried out this kind of assessment in the Galic trial too, or did he just address such problems as bearing, crater, angle of descent. Is this the first time that the witness has embarked on these psychological background type of reports? I see that again the OTP are again springing to their feet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, for the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting, I don't think this is a laughing matter, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not Mr. Whiting, it's Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, again the characterisation of his analysis, military analysis as psychological analysis is, in my submission, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm going allow him to answer it. Did you give similar evidence in Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Galic case, the evidence I gave again was to confirm the reports I was given from the craters; direction of fire, again, angle of descents, likely firing positions and probable military intent. So, yes, the same headings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on specifically to questions about weapons and everything else in relation to these three incidents. Let us begin with this introduction that you made. Above all, all of these things that you say about mortars. This is page two of your report. You make an assessment there and you say, the maximum range would be between 4500 and 7500 metres and most mortars can achieve these ranges by selection of augmenting cartridges normally one to six. Can you, please, first of all, tell me this: Primarily I'm refer here to the incident on the 28th of August. Was there any indication for you to -- that led you to ascertain what sort of a cartridge, what charges were used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the reports, the investigation reports, they determine the calibre of the round, but, no, they could not confirm which charge was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you were never really able to apply any truly accurate method to establish what the range was for any of these 120-millimetre mortars, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these incidents, all I had was the angle of descent, and so then we have to plot back from the point of strike and look at all the different possible firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to move through a number of things quickly. All right. Let's move on to page 3. Page 3 in English too. You speak about the fact that the accuracy of a weapon hinges on several factors, you talk about the tail-fin of the mortar round, the size of the charge, the angle, the direction, stability of the base plate, prevailing weather conditions and you go on to state a number of other factors. Finally you speak about pre-recorded targets. Therefore, we can conclude that you list about ten different factors which the accuracy of a weapon hinges on. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last of all these, the 10th, to be more specific is pre-recorded targets. Maybe that's not on a scale of importance but it is the number ten on this list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is but they're not, as you said, in any list of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I followed very closely the examination-in-chief yesterday. I believe I remember clearly that several factors were pointed out and you explained about stability of the base plate. What I wish to avoid is shuffling my papers now, just to pinpoint the exact reference. But you say that certain places were defined strictly by using weapons throughout the long years of war, and these positions were never changed. How did you establish that locations or positions at which certain weapons were placed were not changed for years? How could you possibly arrive at a conclusion like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where a mortar has been put in position and a -- then set up, if there is no need to move that position, it doesn't make military sense to move it. Because they take time to set up, time to re-supply, and once you have recorded all your recorded targets, if you then move the mortars, those records targets become invalid straight away. So, if you've got a position where you can leave them in one position for a length of time, that would be a massive advantage to any commander. So it's from that point of view and these lines were fixed for such a period of time that gives me my -- the opinion that mortars would have been left as much as possible in their existing positions for as long as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, the confrontation lines remained virtually the same throughout the war. That much is true. But this is not about having a set confrontation line. I'm talking about weapons. How did you establish that certain weapons were always position in the same way, even when not strictly along the confrontation line? What did you base that particular claim on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as I just said, the claim is from military experience and using of mortars and indirect fire weapons, that you do not move them unless you have to. I have got no evidence that says a particular mortar was left in a certain position for two, three years. I don't have that. It is from my opinion and military sense and the way in which they are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, Mr. Higgs, you should know one thing, and I have no alternative but to tell you. Under military rules and precisely for military reasons, it is it necessary indeed, to often change positions taken by certainly weapons. If you remain in the same place for too long you are likely to soon become a target yourself. Would that not seem to be a truism? Please answer, don't just nod your head. In certain weapon systems, yes, that is true, but with a mortar commander especially like in a defensive type environment which this was with fixed [indiscernible] lines then any commander will tell you that from a defensive operations your indirect fire assets are sighted and recorded targets with all the different types of fire recorded, because you will need those weapons to be able to respond immediately. If you keep moving your weapons systems around you loose all your recorded targets. You loose all the advantages of that. You have to re-supply your weapons with all the heavy ammunition into new positions on a regular basis. You then have to re-bed in your mortars which means you have you to fire them to do so, which you then could possibly give their position away in a new position anyway. So you are far better off leaving them in a good position which has cover, where you have sighted originally until such time as you have to move them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about seven years, right? Isn't it a fact that if you use a weapon at a certain position, you should normally leave that position as quickly as possible in order to avoid being eliminated yourself. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an attack situation then that would normally be the case with some type of systems. However, with mortars that is not the case. You move them as and when required to do so by the commander. Mortars do not move unless commanded to do so. It is even a common drill in mortar platoons even when coming under effective fire, they do not move, because they will sustain heavier casualties while in the open moving than they would staying where they are. However, they do move from time to time, but in this -- again, this environment for all of the reasons I've already stated, if you could leave them in one place as long as possible, you get far more advantages. And with all of numbers of good positions, especially in this area, some of the positions you could quite easily have left mortars there for quite a considerable length of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, just a minute. Witness, the question -- the question asked by the Defence, this is about the military snipers. Their job is to touch the target directly. Now on the military point of view, would you say that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that. Would you say that the soldiers are afraid of the snipers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to find out is whether from a tactical point of view, would you say that the people who are in charge of handling the mortars might be afraid of snipers? I'm referring specifically to the distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would be. That is why when sighting the mortgage positions, as I mentioned before, you would keep them away from the confrontation lines as far as possible away from possible sniper activity, and if you could hide them again in dead ground or behind a hillside so they're out of direct line of sight, you take away that threat straight away. That is why most mortar positions, you tend to put them probably a kilometre at least away from the enemy to take away the threat of snipers and to put them into dead ground or behind hillsides or far enough away so small arms fire -- they are out of range of all small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So that explanation might justify, might explain why the mortars are kept in one place for a long time and not moved around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they are in a good position behind a hill or a couple of kilometres, let's say, away from the town where there was no threat to them at all from snipers, then it would not make sense to move them unless you really had to for some tactical reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, pre-recorded targets feature very prominently in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know very well, and it's something that I'm putting to you, that the only thing that can be pre-recorded as a target is the direction and the distance of a target; that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's incorrect. When you record a target, you record the direction to the target, the elevation to the target, the type of ammunition fired at it, the charge fired at that target. If there was a fuse setting, you would record the fuse setting. You also would record the eight figure or the most accurate grid reference to that target as well and also record the altitude of the target. You record all information to the target, not just a bearing to the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you are saying that the sighting equipment used on a mortar can absorb countless elements and use them to target, in addition to such elements as distance to the target or indeed the direction. You are saying that the sighting equipment is actually capable of absorbing other types of information, in order to then use it for targeting, for firing. Is that what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The sight of a mortar will only give you the elevation and the bearing to the target. The other information you get from your map work that would be carried out when engaging target, so you can get your information from the map of the altitude and the grid reference to the target. If you are lucky enough to have any form of basic computer system in the command post, then that of course can do the information for you. But you do not have to have a computer system. You can do it manually using maps for the rest of your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do these pre-recorded targets include systematic errors, those inherent to all systems such as the inaccuracy of weapons? Is this something that is taken into account when recording these targets, the margin of error pertaining to certain weapons, especially in terms of how a weapon is used or how old a certain weapon is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why you pre-record a target is to try, where possible, to shoot out, as they would term it, as many errors as possible, so that when you then come to re-engage that target at a later time, the fire is then more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I hope you're sufficiently familiar with the lie of the land in and around Sarajevo to know that this is a hilly area, a mountainous area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we not say that in a mountainous setting, in a hilly setting such as Sarajevo, of all of the factors that you enumerate about some of those, I think the most important factor is the weather conditions. Could we say that or not? And these weather conditions are not something that is not the kind of information that can be pre-integrated into this list of pre-recorded targets and nobody can do it, is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct that weather does have effect on where the round goes. However, it is possible when recording a target, depending what systems you have, to account for the weather system. Some of the basic computer systems in the command posts at that time were able to take into account the weather, but if you then didn't have those systems, then the weather is always going to be a factor that you cannot determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that a round, once it is fired, especially when dealing with 120-millimetre rounds, being fired from 2.400 metres, it must reach an altitude of between two and three kilometres, it would be expected to, wouldn't it, in order to reach its target?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Depending on the elevation it's is fired on, but, yes, the mortar would go up a fair distance, one or two kilometres. I can't be exact without looking at the range tables, but yes, they will go up a fair distance into the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will be coming to that as well. But there's something else I'd like to ask you. Whatever happens to a round during its actual flight in terms of humidity, any wind, the changing temperature, is this a factor in defining a pre-recording target, nobody can predict humidity, the changing wind, the changing temperature, and there is always wind in a mountainous area, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert, are you familiar with this: This is a piece of information that I have come across in relation to this. Every 100 metres in terms of altitude the temperature changes by 0.6 degrees. Is this something that you're familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the change in temperature with altitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, under such circumstances, how important is what is plotted in the notebook of a commander of such a battery at the moment when he decides to fire? He absolutely has no way of predicting all these weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The altitude issue wouldn't be that important, because that would be the same altitude while the mortar stayed in that position throughout. But whenever that mortar is firing on whatever target, you can use data from firing on to a different target on the same day as you may fire on to another target to find out how the weather conditions are affecting that particular round. But you are correct: If you have not fired a weapon for some time and the weather has changed, then, yes, that is a -- an error which is difficult to calculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that in any event, when you change targets, you don't always shoot at the same target. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You don't always shoot at the same target, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So whenever you select a new target, you have to feed new information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, but any errors you have found on your first target, you can use those to help you with the second one to make it more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, speaking about the rules governing the use of mortars in all armies, are they more or less the same, with reference to 82- and 120-millimetre mortars? Is it true that this is the same in the army of the UK, Russia and other counties and that the same tables of-- firing tables are being used by these armies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every type of ammunition have their own range tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking precisely about the firing tables for M74 mortar, which is 120 millimetres. Is it more or less the same in all armies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The M74 range tables are basically the same. It then depends on which type of ammunition you're firing to make sure you use the data applicable to that type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The other day I was provided by the Prosecution with these range tables. You have seen the 1982 tables of the JNA for the light mortar, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 82 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My apologies. But, yes, let's first begin with 120, but I also want to here about the 82-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've been shown the range tables for the 82 millimetre and the 120 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the deviation at the point of firing for this particular mortar is 16 metres and in terms of distance is between 20 and 35 metres? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the deviation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The deviation of the trajectory of the fire at the moment it is being fired. Now, let me put it straightforwardly to you. Is it true that there are even eight areas of dispersion, according to these tables, and that the deviation in first shells goes as far as 128 metres in direction and up to 312 metres in distance if you take it strictly according to the tables. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These deviate -- all mortars have these deviations, or accuracy, and of course on their first round these tend to be bigger of course than subsequent rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the research conducted with regard to these tables, is it true if you want to hit a target ten by ten, you need at least 139 shells in order to eventually hit the target of the size ten by ten? Abiding only by the rules in place.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reality that is not the case, because it depends on the charge you are firing. On the minimum charges, the lower charges the accuracy is greater. On the higher charges, again the accuracy is quite big. But yes, you do have this worst-case deviation with all mortars on accuracy on all calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if that is the case, please, how was it possible with all these elements contributing or affecting the accuracy and everything else that is written in the tables, how was it possible for a target to be hit with a single round, with a single mortar shell? And I'm talking about Markale, the Markale incident now. And I'm not going to repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem that we have is of course we don't know whether or not they were trying to put that round where it landed outside the front of that building or whether they were actually trying to put it in the market which is a few metres away. We don't know. But all you can do with mortars is try and make them as accurate as possible, like I said before, by recording targets having fixed base plates and so on, to try to keep all these errors to a minimum. That's all can you do. But trying to guarantee to put a round within, as you said, a ten metre by ten metre square, would be nearly impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me mention another characteristic of a 120-millimetre mortar shell. There's an explanation in the rules about that. Is it true that when this shell explodes, it is disintegrated into between 2.500 and 3.000 pieces of shrapnel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The precise number of pieces, I could not confirm, but they are designed to break into smaller pieces than artillery shells, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you speak about this issue on page 4 in English and also page 4 in the B/C/S version when you are talking about the effectiveness of mortars. This is what you say: "Very small place -- at very close range shrapnel can pass through one person and into another." What kind of space are we talking about in which this kind of thing can occur?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To get the larger pieces to pass through one person to another will be happening closer to the point of impact, probably within 20 metres of the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But towards the end of paragraph 1 on page 4 you say as follows: "Shrapnels varies in size. For some pieces it may be centimetres in length, two millimetres in size, very small. In other words, the largest ones measure just a few centimetres or even measure -- or can even be measured in millimetres." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they come in a variety of sizes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the rules that we are talking about stipulate and provide a calculation and they can serve as a basis for certain information that the level of fatality is possible within 17 metres from the place of the landing of the shell, 17 metres? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Levels of fatality are not an accurate science, but of course they can be from the point of impact out to, in cases of the 120, out to 40 or 50 or even 60 metres. I'm not clear what you were meaning by your distance of 17 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I meant was the area around the place of impact and that it can be very accurately calculated on the basis of the rules. And can I give you the reference to the rule. I don't know if you paid attention to it. It's page 29. It speaks about mortar shells and by taking into account certain elements, it can be accurately calculated. My question is: Is it true that based on these parameters, we can say that the area of complete safety begins beyond 35 metres and that all the kinetic energy in the shrapnel is lost and therefore unable to cause casualties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a difficult statement to confirm, because complete safety, you would definitely not have at 35 metres, because even the smaller mortar calibres, 81, 82-millimtre mortars, they have a danger area for complete safety of 190 metres which we use for training, because anything below that, there is a possible chance you may get hit by one piece of shrapnel. So 35 metres is very close it a point of impact, especially with a 120-millimetre. A complete, safe distance would be a lot further away than 35 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to what you said about the shrapnel being able to go through one person and injure another. This can only happen when they are close to the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if there were people on that spot, as stipulated in the indictment, then the closest group of people made it impossible to a great extent for shrapnel to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the last statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please repeat the last part of your question. We didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Provided that there was a large crowd of people, as has been described, and in view of the size of the shrapnel varying from several centimetres to several millimetres, wouldn't it be the case that the bodies of the people would be an obstacle for the majority of pieces of shrapnel and stop them from penetrating further? Is that possible, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true what you already mentioned, that once a shell hits the ground, it affects the area in all directions equally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the angle of descent, but if the round was coming in on a very steep trajectory, then, yes, the blast would be more uniform all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how powerful the blast of the shell is? Can it knock down a person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, depending how far away you are from the point of impact, but if you are close to the impact, then, yes, the blast can knock you over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can it lift you up and threw you away to a certain distance? Because I have seen a photograph where the body of an unfortunate person is on the fence far away from the point of impact. Is it possible for this shell to throw away the person like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the person was standing reasonably close to the blast, then, yes, it would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking generally about incidents, not one of them in particular, in paragraph 1 of your report, which is on page 5 in both versions and it's entitled "Direction of Fire." You say that the direction of fire and establishing thereof is pretty complex and that it depends and relies on a number of various factors. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And further on, when you listed these factors, you said that in addition to the crater, in collecting further evidence, talking to people can be helpful in order to acquire firsthand information about what they either saw or heard.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any of the three incidents that you had an opportunity to analyse, did you find information that there was an eye-witness to any of these shells?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the statements that I have, the statements, the personal accounts of the people on some of the scenes, but really from there, their statements didn't help me in my mortar investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in all cases you at least interviewed witnesses who claimed to have heard the explosion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some of the reports, yes, they heard the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question asked as to whether the witness -- as I understand it, whether the witness interviewed witnesses who claimed to have heard the explosion. I'm not sure whether the -- the witness understood that that was to be the question, that he actually interviewed witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked whether it is fair to say that in all cases you at least interviewed witnesses who claimed to have heard the explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not interviewed anybody, Your Honour. I have only read their written statements as provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was my question and that is exactly what I asked you. I know that this witness did not conduct any investigation. You mostly worked on the documents that were given to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it the time for a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We take the break at 25 minutes to 6.00. So we have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After what I read to you, you say that, "The sound of mortar firing makes it -- is distinctive for anybody who has heard it in action." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a statement here of another expert witness who testified here before you. This is on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, but I don't have the exact reference in the transcript, and I'm sure the Prosecutor will object to my presenting this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness spoke about the whizzing sound of a shell passing through the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be an approximate description of the sound made by a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortar shells do make a noise coming through the air. Not always. But in certain weather conditions they make a sound very similar to how you have described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 4891 of the transcript. This witness even said that this sound is always there and that it even induces people to seek shelter and thereby avoid being hit, because they are anticipating a shell to land.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where you must not get confused between mortars and artillery, because an artillery round that is passing overhead has a very distinctive sound nearly always, and yes, you can obviously hear that. Mortar rounds make a similar sound but not always. It does depend on the weather conditions. But that sound is -- if you like, you hear that sound very shortly before the round strikes the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you can hear it for a number of seconds.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in this particular instance no one had heard the shell being fired, not even those who were at a kilometre from the firing position, and I'm referring now to the observers. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a -- in the report there is no evidence that anybody heard the mortars firing. So, therefore, my conclusion is that obviously the sound must have been muffled in some way. Something must have prevented the sound getting to those people to be able to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But no one heard this projectile flying.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got no reports of anybody hearing anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Neither did the radars record this flight at all, not only this one, you even mention five shells, and nobody ever heard them being fired or flying through the air. How do you explain that? Is it possible in view of the trajectory of a 120-millimetre mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the people not hearing them is concerned, this could be explained if, of course, the mortars were at some distance away hidden behind a hill. As far as the radar is concerned, I'm not an expert on the mortar-locating radar, so I don't know what could have gone wrong, if anything, where they hadn't been detected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs - sorry for interrupting you, counsel - but this is of some importance to our understanding. You are saying that the flying of a mortar after it has been fired only sometimes makes a sound, and I would be curious to know if you can sort of tell us, if you can, whether this is almost always or, in the other scale, rarely that it makes a sound, and what would be the weather conditions which would facilitate the sound and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They tend to make more noise passing through the air when the air is denser, high humidity, those sort of conditions. So it probably happens more often than not rather than rarely, but not every single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just this one thing, a little further down the page you say: "Some people are even able to distinguish different calibres by the sound of a missile or even identify their direction." Not only are they able to identify the sound, they are even able to tell which calibre we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of my statement relates to the firing sound, because, of course, different calibres make different sounds when they are fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please continue. I think you have another -- about another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Higgs, we talked about the sound. We're still on that page. There's that last sentence in that paragraph where you address the issue of sound. "A mortar round only makes a slight noise in flight and you need to be in the right area to hear it and not far from the downward flight path." Well, now, given the situation with one of those incidents, specifically the 28th of August incident, but what I'm asking you is a general question. If one doesn't hear the -- a round being fired at the moment it is fired, if you can't hear it during its flight, not even the slight sound, if you can't even hear it near the spot where the round eventually lands, if you can't hear anything at all before the explosion itself, well, how can you explain that? How can you account for that? Or can that be accounted for, really? Even the radars fail to spot anything, to plot anything.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sound issue can be explained because, as I say, they don't always make an audible sound, depending on the weather conditions, the situation of the people. It could also be affected probably in this case by the buildings or whatever. So sound is a difficult one to quantify. As far as the radar is concerned, I'm not an expert in that field to give an answer of why they were not picked up on the radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am compelled to put to you a hypothesis which is based on these documents. There is, let's say, 100 people who hear an explosion. 95 per cent of them hearing the explosion and some of them hearing a different thing altogether. What could this be a case of? Is that an explosion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, can counsel please repeat the last part of the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the last part of the question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me cut this short. Nothing was heard apart from the explosion. Would that not lead one to conclude that this was something that was planted right there and exploded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basing on the sound issue alone, I think that will be very dangerous to assume that, because, as I said before, you do not always hear the sound for different reasons, so I could not confirm that will be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a hypothesis on my part. We will be going back to a specific incident in a couple of minutes. But first let me clear up a couple of questions with regard to what happened on the 18th of June, 1995. The English page is 15 and the B/C/S is 15, too. The document number remains the same as the previous one, the one that you still have in front of you, presumably.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you know that the time determined here, the 18th of June, 1995, was a time when the conflict between the two parties was very severe, intense, are you aware that was a period of intense fighting between the two warring sides?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, and I think you do, that the place where this occurred is quite near the confrontation line separating the two warring sides?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the place where this fountain was, the water fountain, the spout where people, as the indictment claims, were queueing for water was a place that effectively could not actually be seen, was not in a direct line of sight of those who allegedly fired at them, simply because they were inside a building. This building was ruined, but they were still inside.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can make that -- or made that determination from the pictures that I could see that were sent to me that as you said, it was a ruined building that this water point was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever it was that was firing, we might say, then, simply didn't see those people queueing up for water, did they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not really something I could really answer. I don't know the answer to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to page 16 of the English; 17 in the B/C/S. The chapter entitled "The Correctness and Methodology of the Investigations." It reads: "In this case there was not a normal mortar bomb crater to be able to analyse and determine direction and angle of descent." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down, "Evidence that -- from the evidence supplied to me, there are no pictures showing the fragmentation marks on the floor so I cannot confirm or deny any of those findings." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we therefore conclude this: The pictures you looked at showed no shrapnel marks on the ground, did they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "The blast marks are visible on the wall, but these on their own do not give me enough detail to work with to confirm the bearing." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've seen that photograph, haven't you? It's a black surface and there's nothing much in it aside from that black surface, is there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph of the one where the round struck, it's a blank wall where the round has struck at the top of the wall when you can just see the blast marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "With the bomb striking the wall 3.2 metres off the floor, determination of bearing is not going to be as accurate as if you had a normal crater on the floor." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Page 19 in the B/C/S and 18 in the English. It reads -- the chapter is the findings of the crater analysis of the wall and its effectiveness, paragraph number 2. "The determination of bearing was made easier due to the surrounding buildings eliminating many other options." To all practical intents, you determined the bearing because there were no buildings in the way of this incoming missile, according to your calculation. Is that not a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, if we look at this wall that was hit by the round, it shows no shrapnel marks, does it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It just shows the point of impact blast on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as an expert, a ballistic expert, can you explain how it is possible, if this place is hit by a round of this calibre, that there is no shrapnel to speak of on the wall or on the ground nearby? Is there a possible explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why there's no strike on the wall obviously is because the way it hit the wall, the top of the wall, the blast would have gone beyond the surface of the wall. That's why nothing could be seen there. If there was going to be any shrapnel marks, they would probably have been on the ground around where the people were. But that's a number of metres away from the point of burst, so their markings would have been obviously not as prominent as they are when a mortar round strikes the ground. From the pictures I had, I had no -- I could see no evidence of the strike on the ground from the pictures I was given. They could have been there, but from the evidence I was presented, I couldn't confirm if they were or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if a round hit this precise place, 3.2 metres above the ground, as has been established, wouldn't it be logical for all of the shrapnel to just do the sort of thing that normally occurs in cases such as these to go up into the air? Isn't that in fact where there is an absence of shrapnel here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would explain the absence of some of the shrapnel, yes. But because of the angle of the round as hit the wall, because it's hit it not coming straight down, it's hit on one side, some of the shrapnel would have come down into where obviously the people were as indeed has happened and caused the casualties in that area. But, yes, a lot of the shrapnel would have gone probably over their heads and missed them altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. But you found no shrapnel marks on the ground in those photographs, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the evidence I was given, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Finally I could perhaps ask you this: At the end of this paragraph in relation to determining the direction of fire, and this is on page 19; the English page is 19. It reads: "As I have explained above, this method cannot be confirmed or denied due to the evidence I have, due to what the investigators established during their on-site investigation." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of things about Livanjska. I'm talking about what occurred on the 8th of November, 1994. A crater photograph, 591, P591. Mr. Higgs, if you look at this fan of shrapnel marks in this photograph, how can that be explained? You used these arrows to mark that. How is it possible? How is it possible at all for marks like these not to be there even to a greater extent in the other direction from which the round came? What about the energy generated by this round? Is it not primarily directed against this surface? Yet, in addition to this first circle, there are no shrapnel marks fanning out from the exact spot where the round met the ground or hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the picture, you have the initial crater around the point of impact, which, of course is caused by the initial blast of the bomb exploding. You've then got the -- just away from that, the second crown or this fan caused by the shrapnel coming from the main body of the round. Because the round has come in at an angle, the shrapnel from the other side of the bomb, i.e., on the side nearest us looking at that photograph, that shrapnel of course has missed the ground and has travelled obviously at some distance but without touching the ground because of the angle of descent. That is why you get that particular pattern with this fan shape only on the one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that cast some doubt on your own theory when you said that this fan-like shape would have to spread -- would have to encompass the entire micro area hit by this shell in the form of a circle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the greatest blast is coming from the centre of the body, that is where you see the largest destructive pattern, as you can see here in the second crown. It would be impossible to have that pattern going all the way around, and the nearest you will get to that is if the round was to come down perfectly perpendicular, straight down onto the ground. Then you would have a uniform pattern all the way around, but it would look completely different to this one. This one obviously shows a round has come in at an angle, so you've only got the pattern on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be more logical for the round to have come in from a different direction and the fan-like marks, precisely because of the kinetic energy going in that direction, was left here the way it was? Can we entirely rule the possibility that the round came in from a different direction altogether?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With a good pattern like this one is, the direction is coming from -- as on this picture the central stake that the authorities have laid on the grouped, that is where the round has come in. And that is why we use these patterns to determine the direction of mortar fire, because it has been ballistically proven that these are the patterns that you get, and if the round had come in from a different direction, the pattern on the ground would obviously be orientated in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are therefore categorically stating that this is the only direction that the round could have arrived from, given what the photograph shows you. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P595, please. I'd like you to take a look at that one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, here you marked the direction of the round that was fired at 1525 hours. Can you point out the spot for our benefit that the round was fired from, that was fired at 1730 hours? Can you please draw that for us, mark that for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. 1730 hours, the approximate area would have been somewhere in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: An arrow, please, to indicate the direction between Livanjska and the spot from which the round was fired.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be approximately that direction, which is about 70 degrees, as reported in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be pretty much consistent with UNPROFOR reports claiming that the round arrived from territory held by the BH army, doesn't it? Your arrow, is it supposed to end right here or does it continue beyond the point that you marked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrow shows just the direction. It doesn't show the place of firing. The place of firing in my report suggests the most likely position is the area around the blue circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You will remember what we talked about at the very beginning, at the outset today, those photographs that you were given a short while ago. Do you still believe that you can categorically rule out the possibility that the round arrived from territory held by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I expressed earlier, range is of course difficult to confirm, because at the angle of descent at this location, it would have been possible for all six charges to have the same angle of descent. So I have then used my experience and looking at the confrontation maps to look at most likely firing areas, and at the closer ranges all the positions are in urban areas, residential areas until you get up to the confrontation lines. Again, putting the mortar on or in the confrontation lines would be tactically unsound, and then of course we have the area beyond the confrontation line. Again, because I have no reports of anybody hearing the mortar firing, would suggest it possibly wasn't fired in an urban area, because nobody at all heard it, and again because of the timing and it being dark at this time of year, nobody seeing this muzzle flash would hint it was probably in a more rural area hidden behind a hill somewhere. When you go along that direction, really, the first time you come to that sort of area is the area that I have marked in the blue circle. Prior to that, it is either an urban area, residential areas, or crossing or in the confrontation line areas. And it was from that that I determined that that was the most likely area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that you were asked is whether you still believe that you can categorically rule out the possibility that the round arrived from territory held by the BH army. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot categorically rule it out, Your Honour. This is obviously an opinion I have from experience. Because the mortar could have been fired from six different locations, one for every charge. But the most logical position, because no sound and no sight of it firing, would put it in the area of my blue circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, you have gone past the time allocated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a couple of questions about Markale and one last question about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, ask them quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just my luck. It appears that I'm unable to do it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But about this problem, on the 18th of June, this was the time of the fiercest fighting, even night-time fighting. There's information indicating that. Does that have anything to do your assessments? It was night-time ... Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of June incident happened during the day, so obviously the muzzle flash wouldn't be an issue there, because you can't see it as well during the day. But, of course, it would have the same implications about sound, but if this -- as you say, this was a time of a lot of fighting, there was probably a lot of noise going on, so to identify a single bang within many others would probably prove difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me comply with the instructions of the Presiding Judge. But I do have to ask you this about Markale: You referenced here all the documents that you used. And my question is in relation to any of the incidents. Have you ever tried to obtain any reports from the radar teams monitoring these events which simply must have recorded some of these events? Apparently, not Markale but maybe the other two. Have you ever tried to obtain any sort of information whatsoever from those teams, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reports here have only been put together using the evidence as recorded here on my reports. I have not been given any other supporting evidence regarding the radars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you still categorically support your own claim about Markale despite the report by Harry Konings and his team on the 25th of May, the same team on the 29th, and everything that is contained in the document that was submitted to Kofi Annan on the 29th of September. Despite everything stated in these documents regarding the bearing and the angles and all the assessments showing nothing in terms of the direction of fire because the specific charge is still unfamiliar, the explosive with which the round was filled, do you still stand by your previous claim that the place that the round was fired from was at a distance of 2.400 metres from the place that was eventually hit? I believe Mr. Sachdeva has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the counsel has mentioned quite a few documents, one of them being the report by Harry Konings, and his question is that despite everything stated in this documents regarding the bearing and the angles and all the assessments showing nothing in terms of the direction of fire and my recollection is that Harry Konings's report precisely did make a recording of the direction of fire. So it -- in my submission, it misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that case, then, Mr. Tapuskovic, you'd have to reformulate the question omitting the reference to the Harry Konings report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can do is to show him the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us deal with it -- witness, let us deal with it quickly. Forget the reference to Harry Konings' report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. You were talking at the same time. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I said forgetting the reference to the Harry Konings report, what would your answer to the question be, the question put by counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same as the other incident, I can confirm the bearing with some degree of accuracy, but the range is difficult again because of the charge system that mortars have. So I have to look at the possible options and out of all the possible options, the most likely one is the area of -- range of 2400 because again the one at 900 was close in within again an urban area, surrounded by houses and also marked on one of the other confrontation maps in a minefield, which probably wouldn't be the best place of putting a mortar. The second range puts it right on the confrontation line, which again probably wouldn't be the best place to put it. Which then leaves the maximum ranges, of which 2400 would be the ideal one because of its topological sighting, roads near to it, other positions being near to it, and so on. That is why I concluded that that is the most likely position, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this position drawn on the map be saved as a Defence exhibit and given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a few questions. Can we just keep the map D176?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, can you, I presume with a red pen --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it possible to go back to the Defence exhibit? Mr. Higgs, while that's coming up, let me ask you one question. In the beginning of the cross-examination learned counsel was asking whether you had conducted mortar investigations during wartime, and my question to you is this: With respect to crater examinations, would it matter whether it was done during wartime or peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The methodology carried out is exactly the same. The only advantage in peacetime is of course you can carry out a more thorough examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we're still waiting, I can move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On page 51, counsel for the Defence asked you with respect to the Markale incident, "Mr. Higgs, were you never really able to apply any truly accurate method to establish what the range was for any of these 120-millimetre mortars, were you, sir?" And your answer was: "For these incidents all I had the angle of descent and the -- I think it's bearing," and you then plotted back the different firing positions. And my question to you is: During the course of your career conducting crater examinations and ascertaining the likely firing positions, did you do these investigations without knowing the specific charge? In other words, can you still come to a conclusion as to the possible firing position without knowing the charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we try to do because we always know there is a combination of charges that can give you the same elevation. We then have to in most cases then start looking at likely firing positions going back down the bearing, looking where the most likely place you would put a mortar would be, and that's really how we come to our decision on the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And following on from that question, with respect to -- you've already told the Court that you are not an expert in radar or Cymbelline and therefore, when you conducted your investigations in your career, did you consider radar or Cymbelline reports to come to your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never really used them before. Most of the investigations that I have been part of have never had those in the area, so I just worked from the evidence that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the other question is on page 62 for the Defence's benefit, counsel asked you whether -- well, your answer to a question as to whether one can target a ten metre by ten metre target square and your answer was that it would be nearly impossible to guarantee that target to be engaged. And my question to you is, given your evidence about the pre-recording of targets, the use of observers, in your opinion, could the marketplace have been hit on the first round?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been. There's obviously lots of factors to take into account, all the accuracy issues as already been mentioned. But you still could have been able to get one in that particular size because of course the market is lot bigger than ten metres by ten metres, but it would depend, as I say, on lots of different factors which of course we don't know about. But yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And lastly now we have the picture, or the map on the screen. Can you with a red pen, I think, can you just put the letters FP in the blue circle indicating the firing position, the likely firing position.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And because of a question from counsel, can you extend the arrow to the middle of the circle, lest there be any confusion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender that into evidence, or may have that admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's is my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Higgs, that concludes your -- sorry, Judge Harhoff has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so far, Mr. Higgs. I have a question relating to the device that triggers the explosion of a mortar round. My impression is that there is a fuse at the nose of the round so that when the round hits the ground, then it goes off.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, how much does it take to trigger that? Say you stand up and you just drop the round from a metre and a half, would it then go off?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you -- and -- because I'm asking this because the Defence case has been that the bomb or the mortar was planted. And so one might, at least theoretically, pay some attention to the idea that perhaps it was thrown out of the window from the third floor of the -- some of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a device --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would that have -- yeah, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a device in the fuse for safety reasons in case you drop the ammunition out the back of the lorry on the floor prevents it from exploding. Two devices: Most fuses have some form of safety pin which is removed prior to the round going down the barrel, but also, inside the fuse there are no inertia settings inside the fuse which do not arm until the round is fired. From the inertia of the round firing, going out the barrel at, depending what charge, 150 to 200 and 300 metres per second, that initial action, the thrust from the force of these two inertia bearings backwards on the fuse. If you don't have that, it will not arm. If you take one out and drop it on the floor, it will not explode. So that's why making a round explode that has been suspended somehow on the ground, it would take some setting up to have some form of initiation device, because the fuse in itself would not be good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. So even if you were to throw it out of the window from the third floor, the round would not explode?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not have had enough inertia to set the safety devices in the fuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And just for my understanding, the charges that you apply to a mortar, is that a separate component from the mortar itself, from the grenade itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- or is it a part of --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are completely separate. They do detach. Normally when most mortar rounds are delivered, when they come in their box, they will come fully charged with all four, six, or eight charges, depending on what type of mortar they are, already on the tail system. You would then take off the ones that you don't need. If you're firing on four charge, you leave them all on. If you're only firing on charge two, let's say, then you'll take them all off apart from the bottom two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you put down the tube in a mortar barrel is the mortar itself with a number of charges attached to it underneath.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that how it works?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's why people call -- sometimes call them cheeses, because they're shaped like a horseshoe with a lot of munitions, and they just slide over the tail section, so they would be already connected to the tail section as you place it down the barrel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, that does in fact now conclude your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Docherty is taking the next witness. Might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, Mr. Docherty, next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Mr. Milomir Soja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Soja. Could you please introduce yourself to the Judges by telling them your name and also what you do for a living just now.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: My name is Milomir Soja. I'm an electrical engineer, and currently I work at the Faculty of Electronics in eastern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Soja, I'm going to be ask you some questions concerning some work you did on the ignition systems of modified aerial bombs in 1995, and I want to begin by talking about the qualifications that you brought to that work. Could you please tell Their Honours what your education is, including the years that you graduated, and the subjects that you specialised in.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: I completed my primary and secondary schools in Ilidza. In 1982, I graduated from the Faculty of Electrical Engineering in Sarajevo. After that, up until the war, I had been working with Energoinvest factory in the department of electronics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say that you worked for Energoinvest, can you tell Their Honours what kind of company Energoinvest is and what it was that you did there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Energoinvest is a big company. I worked in a small department employing around 90 people, and the company I worked for was in the field of energy and electronics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that where you were working when the armed conflict broke out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you serve in the armed forces during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, lastly, is it correct that you were released from the armed forces on the last day of 1994, that is to say, 31st December?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SOJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
